recent_posts.title: Breadboard and Opal
recent_posts.summary: Breadboard is an open source project for composing AI patterns through graph-based systems, serving as the foundation for Google's Opal product. This follows a common pattern where open source projects become the backbone of commercial products, similar to how Chromium powers Chrome. The author explains how this relationship allows broader impact by making AI composition tools accessible to more developers while maintaining a clear distinction between the open source project and the commercial product built upon it.

recent_posts.title: Machine Thinking
recent_posts.summary: Large language models (LLMs) simulate human thought processes by navigating complex terrains of mental models. However, unlike humans, LLMs think without an inherent drive for homeostasis or emotional experiences. While LLMs can imitate human thinking and produce similar outcomes, their underlying mechanisms are fundamentally different. Understanding these distinctions is crucial for harnessing the true potential of LLMs without misinterpreting their capabilities.

recent_posts.title: Recipes for Thought
recent_posts.summary: The post discusses two approaches to interacting with large language models (LLMs): the 'chat' approach, which involves a traditional back-and-forth conversation, and the 'recipe' approach, which sees each interaction as steps in a structured process. The author suggests that the recipe approach can lead to better results by refining the prompts and shaping the conversation turns more deliberately. This method engages metacognition, helping users understand their own and the LLM's thinking processes. The post also highlights how repeatable thinking recipes can scale cognitive know-how and improve productivity.

recent_posts.title: Teaching AI to write lyrics
recent_posts.summary: Exploring the process of using large language models (LLMs) to generate creative lyrics, this post outlines several techniques and methodologies to improve the quality and creativity of the outputs. It begins with simple prompt requests and evolves through structured approaches such as the 'lyrical factory' and the 'loosey-goosey duo.' The journey highlights the use of 'reminding the model' technique, Plan + Execute pattern, and few-shot prompting, supplemented by human oversight and a semantic store of existing lyrics. Despite significant improvement, the quest for high-quality AI-generated lyrics continues.

recent_posts.title: Jamming with Udio
recent_posts.summary: Udio introduces audio prompting for jam sessions, allowing users to use their own sound as a starting point for a generated track. The process involves extending existing audio clips, matching the prompt's tempo and style, and adding new details to create a cohesive track.

recent_posts.title: The third option
recent_posts.summary: The post discusses the concept of lensical thinking and how it can be applied to solve unsolvable problems. It explores the idea of polarities and the need for a third option. The third option allows for a different perspective and more room to navigate polarities.

recent_posts.title: Flexibility of the medium
recent_posts.summary: The post discusses the experiment of transforming blog posts into lyrics and then into short songs using generative AI. It explores the flexibility of medium transformation and the possibilities it opens up for creative expression. The author highlights the rapid iteration process and the potential for a new era of UX explorations.

recent_posts.title: The Bootstrapping Phase
recent_posts.summary: The bootstrapping phase refers to a period in a product's life where it is not yet good enough to help users, but needs user feedback. Assumptions about the product's final shape are tested and changed during this phase. There is a collaborative relationship between the product creators and users, with users being full participants in the product's development.

top_posts.title: Fix-forward and rollback commit stances
top_posts.summary: Dimitri Glazkov: Fix-forward and rollback commit stances work well in smaller projects. He says the fix-forward stance places the responsibility of fixing the bad code on the collective shoulders of the project members. The rollback stance is more appealing, and it scales rather well to large teams with diverse degrees of engagement.
